part: Part A: the floor you cannot skip
title: Powers of Ten, Prefixes and the Seven Steps
lead: Almost every mark lost on this paper is lost before the physics starts. Five of the fifteen options in a PHY121 question are usually the SAME digits with different powers of ten, so the exponent is the thing being marked. This lesson makes that automatic.

blocks.html:
Look at what Test 2 question 8 actually offers you: 7.58 x 10-4, 7.58 x 10-6, 7.58 x 10-2, 7.58 x 10-8, 7.58 x 10-1. Identical digits. The examiner has already granted you the physics and is marking one thing only: whether you can handle the powers of ten.

That is the pattern across this course. Get this lesson right and you stop losing marks you had already earned.

blocks.label: The prefixes you must know cold
blocks.html:
PrefixSymbolMultiply by
picop10-12
nanon10-9
microµ10-6
millim10-3
centic10-2
kilok103
megaM106
gigaG109

The three that appear constantly in PHY121: micro for charge and capacitance, nano for small capacitors and charges, pico for the smallest capacitors.

blocks.label: The centimetre trap
blocks.html:
A distance in centimetres squared is the single most expensive slip in this course. Test 1 question 4 gives r = 5 cm. If you put 5 into kQ/r you get a potential 100 times too small, and 20 cm gives one 400 times too small.

5 cm is 0.05 m, and 0.05 squared is 0.0025. Convert the moment you read the number, before you write anything else down.

blocks.label: Powers of ten, one step at a time
blocks.tag: cover the page and slide down
blocks.howto: Read the teaching step, do the small task at the end of it, then move to the next frame, which opens with the answer. Do not read ahead.

frames.teach: To multiply powers of ten, ADD the exponents. 10<sup>3</sup> times 10<sup>4</sup> is 10<sup>7</sup>.
frames.ask: What is 2 x 10<sup>-6</sup> multiplied by 3 x 10<sup>-3</sup>?

frames.check: 6 x 10<sup>-9</sup>. Multiply the front numbers, 2 times 3 = 6, then add the exponents, minus 6 plus minus 3 = minus 9.
frames.teach: To divide, SUBTRACT the bottom exponent from the top one. 10<sup>5</sup> divided by 10<sup>2</sup> is 10<sup>3</sup>.
frames.ask: What is 8 x 10<sup>-4</sup> divided by 4 x 10<sup>-7</sup>?

frames.check: 2 x 10<sup>3</sup>. Divide the front numbers, 8 over 4 = 2, then subtract, minus 4 minus minus 7 = plus 3.
frames.teach: Watch what happens when the front division gives less than 1. 3.64 over 4.8 is 0.758, which is NOT in standard form, so you shift it to 7.58 and drop the exponent by one to compensate.
frames.ask: Work out (9.1 x 10<sup>-31</sup> x 4 x 10<sup>6</sup>) divided by (1.6 x 10<sup>-19</sup> x 0.03), which is Test 2 question 8.

frames.check: 7.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup> m. Top: 9.1 x 4 = 36.4, and minus 31 plus 6 = minus 25, so 36.4 x 10<sup>-25</sup>, that is 3.64 x 10<sup>-24</sup>. Bottom: 1.6 x 0.03 = 0.048, so 4.8 x 10<sup>-21</sup>. Dividing: 3.64 over 4.8 = 0.758 and minus 24 minus minus 21 = minus 3, giving 0.758 x 10<sup>-3</sup> = 7.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup>.
frames.teach: That last shift, from 0.758 x 10<sup>-3</sup> to 7.58 x 10<sup>-4</sup>, is exactly the step the five options were testing.

frames.check: 10<sup>-4</sup>. The less negative the exponent, the bigger the number. 10<sup>-4</sup> is a ten thousandth, 10<sup>-6</sup> a millionth.
frames.teach: Keep the front numbers and the powers of ten in two separate columns while you work. That is step 6 of the seven-step method, and it is what stops the exponent slipping.

blocks.label: The seven steps
blocks.html:
1. Read the question twice and underline what is asked for.
  2. List what you know, with symbols and units.
  3. Convert everything to SI immediately.
  4. Choose the formula holding what you know and what you want.
  5. Rearrange in symbols first, and substitute numbers only at the end.
  6. Compute, keeping powers of ten separate from the front numbers.
  7. Check: is the size believable, is the unit right, does the sanity check hold?

Read, list, convert, choose, rearrange, compute, check. Steps 3 and 7 save the most marks and are the two most often skipped.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: Convert each to SI: (1) 8 mg, (2) 50 cm, (3) 4.5 nC, (4) 2.25 mJ, (5) 5 pF.
blocks.answer:
(1) 8 x 10-6 kg, because milli is 10-3 and a gram is 10-3 kg. (2) 0.50 m. (3) 4.5 x 10-9 C. (4) 2.25 x 10-3 J. (5) 5 x 10-12 F.

Number 1 catches people twice, because milligrams need BOTH conversions. It is Test 1 question 3.

blocks.sub: Five options with the same digits means the exponent is the question.

title: Charge, Force, Field and Potential
lead: Four formulas carry a third of this paper. The whole difficulty is knowing which one is being asked for, and remembering that the field is squared while the potential is not.

blocks.label: What a field actually is
blocks.html:
A charge does not reach out and touch another charge. It changes the space around it, and the second charge responds to the space it finds itself in. That change in the space is the electric field.

So there are two separate questions, and the paper asks both:

  • What field is there? That depends only on the charge PRODUCING it: E = kQ/r2.
  • What force does a charge feel? That depends on the field and on the charge sitting in it: F = qE.

Test 1 question 13 lives or dies on this distinction. It gives two charges and asks for the field produced by the NEGATIVE one at the location of the positive one. Only the negative charge goes into the formula. The other charge is where you are standing, not what you are measuring.

blocks.label: The four formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
Quantisationq = nee = 1.602 x 10-19 C, n a whole number
Coulomb's lawF = kq1q2/r2Between two charges
FieldE = F/q = kQ/r2Vector. N/C or V/m
PotentialV = kQ/rScalar. Note the plain r

k = 8.99 x 109, used as 9 x 109.

blocks.label: Squared or not squared
blocks.html:
E = kQ/r2 but V = kQ/r.

The field is squared. The potential is not. Test it on yourself: if you move three times further away, the FIELD drops to a ninth but the POTENTIAL drops only to a third.

Test 1 question 4 is built on this. It gives r = 5 cm and r = 20 cm, a fourfold increase, and the potential falls from 720 kV to 180 kV, which is a quarter. If you had squared it you would have looked for a sixteenth and found no such option.

blocks.label: Test 1 question 8, worked in full
blocks.problem: Two charges Q1 = +3.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C and Q2 = -3.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C are placed 0.10 m apart in air. Find the net electric field at the midpoint between the charges.
blocks.working:
Given
Q1 = +3.0 x 10-6 C
Q2 = -3.0 x 10-6 C
separation = 0.10 m, so r to the midpoint = 0.05 m
k = 9 x 109

Formula
E = kQ/r2 for each charge, then add as vectors.

Field from each charge
E = (9 x 109 x 3 x 10-6) / (0.05)2
  = 27000 / 0.0025
  = 1.08 x 107 N/C

Direction, which is the whole question
A field points AWAY from a positive charge and TOWARDS a negative one. Standing at the midpoint, the field from Q1 pushes away from Q1, and the field from Q2 pulls towards Q2. Both point the same way, from Q1 to Q2, so they ADD.

Net field
E = 2 x 1.08 x 107
  = 2.16 x 107 N/C
blocks.redo: Redo it with Q2 changed to +3.0 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C. The magnitudes are identical, but now both fields point outwards from the midpoint in OPPOSITE directions, so they cancel and the net field is zero. That sign change is the whole of superposition.

blocks.label: Which formula does the question want?
blocks.howto: Each frame gives you a question stem. Decide which formula it needs before you slide down.

frames.teach: Read for the QUANTITY asked for and the units offered. Units in N/C or V/m mean a field. Units in volts mean a potential. Units in newtons mean a force.
frames.ask: "A charge of +1.5 x 10<sup>-9</sup> C is placed in a uniform electric field of magnitude 2500 N/C. What is the magnitude of the force?" Which formula?

frames.check: F = qE. The field is GIVEN, so no inverse square is needed at all: F = 1.5 x 10<sup>-9</sup> x 2500 = 3.75 x 10<sup>-6</sup> N. That is Test 1 question 7.
frames.teach: When the field is handed to you, Coulomb's law does not come into it. Students lose this mark by reaching for kQ/r<sup>2</sup> out of habit.
frames.ask: "What is the absolute potential 5 cm from a charge of +4 microcoulombs?" Which formula?

frames.teach: Note that 36000 divided by 0.05 is 720000, not 1800. Dividing by a number less than one makes the answer bigger.
frames.ask: "What is the charge of a system that has 6.2 x 10<sup>18</sup> electrons?" Which formula?

frames.check: q = ne = 6.2 x 10<sup>18</sup> x 1.602 x 10<sup>-19</sup> = 0.99 C. That is Test 1 question 10.
frames.teach: Notice the answer sits just under 1 coulomb. That is because 1/e is about 6.24 x 10<sup>18</sup>, so 6.2 x 10<sup>18</sup> electrons is almost exactly one coulomb. A useful check.
frames.ask: "Calculate the electric field in which an oil drop of mass 8 mg and charge +9 microcoulombs is held stationary." What is the physical condition?

frames.check: Stationary means the forces BALANCE: the electric force up equals the weight down. qE = mg, so E = mg/q.
frames.teach: Now convert: 8 mg is 8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> kg, and 9 microcoulombs is 9 x 10<sup>-6</sup> C. E = (8 x 10<sup>-6</sup> x 10) / (9 x 10<sup>-6</sup>) = 8.89 V/m. The examiner is using g = 10.
frames.ask: Why did the powers of ten vanish so cleanly there?

frames.check: Because 10<sup>-6</sup> appeared on the top and the bottom and cancelled. Spotting that saves the whole calculation.
frames.teach: That is the pattern to look for: when a mass in milligrams meets a charge in microcoulombs, the exponents often cancel.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A charge of 8 x 10-8 C sits 0.40 m from a charge of -2.0 x 10-8 C. Determine the electric field produced by the NEGATIVE charge at the location of the positive charge.
blocks.answer:
Only the negative charge produces the field being asked about, so only it goes into the formula.

E = kQ/r2 = 9 x 109 x 2 x 10-8 / (0.40)2 = 180 / 0.16 = 1125 N/C.

The 8 x 10-8 C charge is where you are standing. If you had used it instead you would have got about four times the answer, which is one of the offered options. Test 1 question 13.

blocks.big: Field is squared, potential is not
blocks.sub: And only the charge PRODUCING the field goes in the formula.

title: Flux, Gauss and Conductors
lead: Flux questions are among the easiest on the paper if you know where the angle is measured from, and Gauss turns a sphere into a point charge in one line.

blocks.text: Flux is just how much field goes through

blocks.label: The rain and the hoop
blocks.html:
Hold a hoop in falling rain. Face it straight up and the most rain falls through. Tilt it and less gets through. Turn it edge on and none does.

Flux is exactly that: how much field passes through a surface. Φ = EA cos θ, and the angle is measured from the normal, the line sticking straight out of the surface, NOT from the surface itself.

So θ = 0 means the field goes straight through and cos 0 = 1, the maximum. θ = 90 degrees means the field skims along the surface and cos 90 = 0, nothing gets through.

blocks.label: Test 1 question 5
blocks.problem: A uniform electric field E = 200 N/C passes through a surface of area 2 m<sup>2</sup> at 0 degrees. Find the flux.
blocks.working:
Given
E = 200 N/C
A = 2 m2
θ = 0 degrees

Formula
Φ = EA cos θ

Substitute
Φ = 200 x 2 x cos 0
  = 200 x 2 x 1
  = 400
blocks.redo: Redo it at 60 degrees. cos 60 = 0.5, so the flux halves to 200. Redo it at 90 degrees and it is zero, because the field never crosses the surface at all.

blocks.label: Gauss in one sentence
blocks.html:
Flux out equals charge in, divided by ε0.

Two consequences the paper uses:

  • A charge OUTSIDE the surface contributes nothing. Every field line it sends in comes back out.
  • Outside a charged sphere, the field is the same as if all the charge sat at the centre. So E = kQ/r2 with r measured from the centre.
  • Inside a hollow conductor the field is zero, because no charge is enclosed. That is the Faraday cage.

blocks.label: From the centre, not the surface
blocks.html:
"A conducting sphere of radius 0.25 m carries 6 x 10-6 C. Find the field at a point 0.50 m from the centre."

The radius is there for one reason only: to tell you 0.50 m is OUTSIDE the sphere, so the point-charge result applies. It does not enter the arithmetic.

E = 9 x 109 x 6 x 10-6 / (0.50)2 = 54000 / 0.25 = 2.16 x 105 N/C.

Adding the radius to the distance, or subtracting it, both produce offered options. Read whether the distance is from the centre or from the surface.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) A closed surface encloses 3 µC. A further 10 µC sits just outside it. What is the net flux through the surface?

(2) What is the electric field deep inside a solid copper block sitting in a strong external field?
blocks.answer:
(1) Φ = Qenclosed/ε0 = 3 x 10-6 / 8.85 x 10-12 = 3.39 x 105 N m2/C. The 10 µC outside contributes nothing.

(2) Zero. Charge rearranges on the surface until the interior field cancels exactly. No enclosed charge, no field.

blocks.big: The angle is from the normal
blocks.sub: And Gauss counts only what is inside.

title: Capacitance, Dielectrics, Networks and Energy
lead: Capacitance came up four times on Test 1, including the only question carrying a diagram. The networks are where the marks are, and reading the picture matters more than the formula.

blocks.label: The bucket
blocks.html:
A capacitor is a bucket for charge, and capacitance is how WIDE the bucket is: how much charge it holds for each volt you apply.

C = Q/V. Charge per volt.

Here is the part that catches people. Widening the bucket is not something you do by pouring more in. Raise the voltage and you push in more charge, but in exact proportion, so the ratio does not budge. Capacitance is fixed by geometry: the plate area, the gap between them, and what sits in the gap. For a parallel plate, C = εrε0A/d contains no Q and no V at all.

blocks.label: The capacitor formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
DefinitionC = Q/VUnit farad
Parallel plateC = εrε0A/dεr = 1 in vacuum
In parallelC = C1 + C2They ADD
In series1/C = 1/C1 + 1/C2Less than the smallest
EnergyW = ½CV2 = ½QV = Q2/2CThree equivalent forms

Capacitors add in parallel. That is backwards from resistors. Learn one and flip it for the other.

blocks.label: Test 1 question 2, the network with the figure
blocks.problem: C1 = 1 µF and C2 = 5 µF sit one above the other in the same branch. That branch spans the same two terminals as C3 = 8 µF. Find the total capacitance.
blocks.working:
Step 1: read the arrangement, before any formula.
C1 and C2 are in the SAME branch, one after the other, so the same charge must pass through both: they are in series.
That branch and C3 span the same two terminals, so they are in parallel.

Step 2: series first.
1/Cs = 1/1 + 1/5
  = 5/5 + 1/5
  = 6/5
Cs = 5/6 = 0.833 µF

Step 3: then parallel, which simply adds.
C = 0.833 + 8
  = 8.83 µF

Step 4: check.
Adding anything in parallel can only INCREASE the total, so the answer had to be above 8. It is.
blocks.redo: Two wrong answers are offered as traps: 0.8 µF is the series step with C3 forgotten, and 14.0 µF is all three added as though everything were parallel. Redo the problem with all three in series and confirm you get less than 1 µF, which is the sanity check for series.

blocks.label: The other three capacitor questions
blocks.howto: Work each step before sliding down to the answer.

frames.teach: Test 1 question 6 gives a parallel plate: area 4 x 10<sup>-2</sup> m<sup>2</sup>, dielectric thickness 10<sup>-3</sup> m, relative permittivity 7. The formula is C = epsilon-r epsilon-0 A / d.
A capacitance in nanofarads is believable. Two of the offered options have POSITIVE exponents, which would be a capacitor larger than any ever built. Step 7 kills them instantly.
frames.ask: Test 1 question 11: a sphere carries 4.5 nC at 180 V above its surroundings. Find its capacitance.

frames.teach: All the talk of spheres and insulating rods is scenery. The moment you see a charge and a voltage, C = Q/V is the whole question.
frames.ask: Test 1 question 15: a capacitor stores 2.25 mJ when charged to 30 V. Find C.

frames.check: W = 1/2 CV<sup>2</sup>, so C = 2W/V<sup>2</sup> = (2 x 2.25 x 10<sup>-3</sup>) / 900 = 4.5 x 10<sup>-3</sup> / 900 = 5 x 10<sup>-6</sup> F = 5 microfarads.
frames.teach: Two things to get right: the factor of 2 when you rearrange, and squaring the 30 to 900. Forgetting the half gives 2.5 microfarads, which is an offered option.
frames.ask: Why is there a half in the energy formula at all?

frames.check: Because the voltage climbed from zero as the capacitor charged. The first charge crossed almost no potential difference, the last crossed the full V, so the average was V/2.
frames.teach: The same argument produces the half in 1/2 LI<sup>2</sup> for an inductor, which you will meet in the induction lesson.

blocks.big: Read the picture, then choose the formula
blocks.sub: Series first, parallel second, and parallel can only make it bigger.

title: Current, Resistance, emf and Internal Resistance
lead: Every circuit question on both tests is Ohm's law plus one idea: a battery has resistance of its own, so what you measure at its terminals is always less than what it can supply.

blocks.text: The one idea behind five questions

blocks.label: Why headlights dim
blocks.html:
Start a car at night and the headlights dip for a moment. The battery has not gone flat. What happened is that the starter motor suddenly drew an enormous current, and a battery has resistance inside itself.

That internal resistance eats some of the battery's voltage before it ever reaches the terminals. The more current you draw, the more it eats.

V = E - Ir

E is the emf, what the battery can supply. r is its internal resistance. V is the terminal voltage, what you actually measure. V is always less than E whenever current flows, and that single sentence answers three questions on Test 2.

blocks.label: The circuit formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
Ohm's lawV = IRCover what you want
Series RR = R1 + R2Same current everywhere
Parallel R1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2Less than the smallest
Two in parallelR = R1R2/(R1+R2)Product over sum
emfE = I(R + r)Drives current through both
Terminal voltageV = E - IrAlways less than E

blocks.label: Which resistance does the question mean?
blocks.html:
Test 1 question 12 asks for "the current that flows through R3" in a series circuit of 7, 6 and 3 ohms across 48 V.

Naming R3 invites you to compute 48/3 = 16 A. But in series the same current flows through everything, so the answer for R3 is the answer for the whole loop: R = 16 ohms, I = 48/16 = 3 A.

The trap works because the question sounds like it is asking about one component. It is not.

blocks.label: Test 2 question 4, the two-step one
blocks.tag: hardest circuit question on the paper
blocks.problem: A cell of unknown emf E and internal resistance 2 ohms is connected to a 5 ohm resistor. If the terminal p.d. is 1 volt, calculate E.
blocks.working:
Given
r = 2 Ω (internal)
R = 5 Ω (external)
V = 1 V (terminal p.d.)
E = ?

Step 1: the terminal p.d. is the voltage across the EXTERNAL resistor, so it gives you the current.
I = V/R
  = 1/5
  = 0.2 A

Step 2: the emf must push that current through BOTH resistances.
E = I(R + r)
  = 0.2 x (5 + 2)
  = 0.2 x 7
  = 1.4 V

Check
E = 1.4 V is greater than V = 1 V, as it must be. The difference, 0.4 V, is the internal drop Ir = 0.2 x 2. It agrees.
blocks.redo: The offered trap is 1 V, the terminal p.d. copied straight out of the question. Whenever a question gives you a terminal p.d. and asks for emf, the answer must be BIGGER. Redo it with r = 5 ohms and confirm you get 2 V.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question: A cell has an emf of 9 V and an internal resistance of 1 ohm. The current flowing is 2 A. What is the terminal voltage?
blocks.answer:
V = E - Ir = 9 - (2 x 1) = 7 V.

This is the previous question run backwards: there you were given V and asked for E, here you are given E and asked for V. Either way the terminal voltage is the smaller of the two. An answer of 11 V would mean the internal resistance was ADDING energy, which is impossible.

blocks.sub: What you measure is always less than what the battery has.

title: Magnetic Force, Circular Paths and Torque
lead: One formula with a sine in it, and one consequence: because the force is always sideways, a magnetic field bends a charge into a circle without ever changing its speed.

blocks.text: Why the path is a circle

blocks.label: A force that only steers
blocks.html:
The magnetic force on a moving charge is always perpendicular to its velocity. Think of swinging a stone on a string: the string pulls sideways, never forwards, so the stone circles at constant speed.

Two things follow, and the paper tests both:

  • Magnetic fields do no work. A sideways force cannot speed anything up, so the kinetic energy never changes. The field steers; it does not accelerate in the everyday sense.
  • The path is a circle, with the magnetic force supplying the centripetal force: qvB = mv2/r, which rearranges to r = mv/(qB).

And because F = qvB sin θ, there are two ways to feel no force at all: stand still (v = 0), or travel straight along the field (sin 0 = 0).

blocks.label: The magnetism formulas
blocks.html:
QuantityFormulaNote
Force on a chargeF = qvB sin θMax at 90 degrees, zero at 0
Radius of the pathr = mv/(qB)Faster means wider
Cyclotron frequencyf = qB/(2πm)No v in it
Force on a wireF = BIL sin θMax at 90 degrees
Magnetic momentm = NIAN turns, area A
Torque on a loopτ = mB sin θZero when aligned

Electron mass 9.11 x 10-31 kg, proton mass 1.67 x 10-27 kg.

blocks.label: Read the angle before you reach for the sine
blocks.html:
Test 2 uses two different angles in two consecutive skills, and the sines are not interchangeable.

  • Question 2 gives 60 degrees, and sin 60 = 0.866.
  • Question 7 gives 30 degrees, and sin 30 = 0.5 exactly.

Dropping the sine altogether in question 2 gives 1.0 x 106, which is NOT among the options, so the examiner has deliberately made the sine the marked step.

blocks.label: Test 2 question 2, worked in full
blocks.problem: A proton experiences a magnetic force of 3.2 x 10<sup>-14</sup> N while moving through a magnetic field of 0.2 T. The angle between the velocity and the field is 60 degrees. Calculate the speed. Take q = 1.6 x 10<sup>-19</sup> C.
blocks.working:
Given
F = 3.2 x 10-14 N
B = 0.2 T
θ = 60 degrees, so sin θ = 0.866
q = 1.6 x 10-19 C
v = ?

Formula, rearranged in symbols first
F = qvB sin θ
v = F / (qB sin θ)

Denominator first, keeping the powers of ten separate
qB sin θ = 1.6 x 10-19 x 0.2 x 0.866
  = 1.6 x 0.2 x 0.866 x 10-19
  = 0.2771 x 10-19
  = 2.771 x 10-20

Divide
v = 3.2 x 10-14 / 2.771 x 10-20
  = 1.155 x 106 m/s
blocks.redo: Redo it at 30 degrees instead. sin 30 = 0.5, so the denominator falls and the speed rises to 2.0 x 10<sup>6</sup> m/s. Redo it again at 90 degrees: sin 90 = 1, giving 1.0 x 10<sup>6</sup> m/s, which is the answer you would wrongly get by forgetting the sine.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
(1) A rectangular loop feels a torque of 4.8 x 10-3 N m in a 0.6 T field, at 30 degrees. Find the magnetic dipole moment.

(2) An electron (9.1 x 10-31 kg, 1.6 x 10-19 C) enters a 0.03 T field perpendicularly at 4 x 106 m/s. Find the radius.
blocks.answer:
(1) τ = mB sin θ, so m = τ/(B sin θ) = 4.8 x 10-3 / (0.6 x 0.5) = 4.8 x 10-3 / 0.3 = 1.6 x 10-2 A m2.

(2) r = mv/(qB) = (9.1 x 10-31 x 4 x 106) / (1.6 x 10-19 x 0.03) = 3.64 x 10-24 / 4.8 x 10-21 = 7.58 x 10-4 m.

Every option in the second one is 7.58 with a different exponent, so it is purely a powers-of-ten question wearing a physics costume.

blocks.big: Magnetic fields steer, they never speed up
blocks.sub: And always read the angle before you use the sine.

title: Where Fields Come From, Induction and Transformers
lead: Wires and coils make fields, changing flux makes emf, and a transformer trades voltage for current. Six marks on Test 2, and one unit trap that catches almost everybody.

blocks.label: The four sources you need
blocks.html:
ArrangementFieldNote
Long straight wireB = µ0I/(2πr)Falls as 1/r
Centre of a loopB = µ0NI/(2R)N turns
SolenoidB = µ0nIn is turns PER METRE
ToroidB = µ0NI/(2πr)N is the TOTAL turns

µ0 = 4π x 10-7. Leave it as 4π, because the π very often cancels.

Biot-Savart gives the field of a tiny current element and falls as 1/r2. Ampere's law is the shortcut, and it is only useful when the arrangement has symmetry.

blocks.label: n is turns per metre, N is total turns
blocks.tag: the biggest trap in this topic
blocks.html:
Test 2 question 9: a solenoid 0.4 m long with 800 turns produces 2.5 x 10-4 T. Find the current.

Put 800 into B = µ0nI and you get the wrong answer, and it is one of the offered options.

n = N/L = 800/0.4 = 2000 turns per metre.

Then I = B/(µ0n) = 2.5 x 10-4 / (4π x 10-7 x 2000) = 2.5 x 10-4 / 2.513 x 10-3 = 0.1 A.

The toroid formula uses total turns, the solenoid formula uses turns per metre. That inconsistency is deliberate on the examiner's part.

blocks.label: Test 2 question 14, and why to keep the pi
blocks.problem: At a distance of 5 cm from a long straight wire, the magnetic field is 4.0 x 10<sup>-5</sup> T. Calculate the current. Use µ<sub>0</sub> = 4π x 10<sup>-7</sup>.
blocks.working:
Given
r = 5 cm = 0.05 m
B = 4.0 x 10-5 T
µ0 = 4π x 10-7

Formula, rearranged first
B = µ0I/(2πr)
I = 2πrB / µ0

Substitute, and notice the π
I = (2π x 0.05 x 4 x 10-5) / (4π x 10-7)

The π cancels top and bottom
I = (2 x 0.05 x 4 x 10-5) / (4 x 10-7)
  = (0.4 x 10-5) / (4 x 10-7)
  = (4 x 10-6) / (4 x 10-7)
  = 10 A
blocks.redo: If you had turned µ<sub>0</sub> into 1.2566 x 10<sup>-6</sup> first, you would have reached the same answer with four times the arithmetic and four times the chance of slipping. Redo it at r = 10 cm and confirm the current doubles to 20 A, because B falls as 1/r.

blocks.text: Induction: change is the whole word

blocks.label: Why a steady field induces nothing
blocks.html:
Faraday's law is emf = -N dΦ/dt. Read the d/dt: it is the rate of change of flux that makes an emf, not the flux itself.

Park a coil in the strongest steady magnet you can find and it generates nothing at all. Move it, or turn it, or switch the field, and it does. That is why a generator has to spin.

Flux is Φ = BA cos θ, so there are three ways to change it: change B, change the area A, or rotate the loop to change θ.

The minus sign is Lenz's law: the induced effect opposes the change that made it. If it reinforced instead, the smallest nudge would grow without limit and make energy from nothing. Nature always fights back.

blocks.label: Induction and transformers
blocks.howto: Work each step before sliding down.

frames.teach: Energy stored in an inductor is W = 1/2 L I<sup>2</sup>. It mirrors 1/2 C V<sup>2</sup> for a capacitor, and the half is there for the same reason: the current climbed from zero.
frames.ask: Test 2 question 1: a 2 H inductor carries 5 A. Find the stored energy.

frames.check: W = 1/2 x 2 x 5<sup>2</sup> = 1 x 25 = 25 J. The current is SQUARED, the inductance is not.
frames.teach: The trap answer is 10 J, which is simply L times I, forgetting both the half and the square.
frames.ask: A transformer has Np = 100, Ns = 1000, Ep = 240 V. Is this a step up or a step down, and what is Es?

frames.check: Ns is greater than Np, so it steps UP. Es = Ep x Ns/Np = 240 x 10 = 2400 V.
frames.teach: The turns ratio equals the voltage ratio: Es/Ep = Ns/Np. Deciding step-up or step-down FIRST eliminates three of the five options before any arithmetic.
frames.ask: Test 2 question 6: a 240 V transformer lights eight 12 V, 24 W lamps and draws 1 A in the primary. Find the efficiency.

frames.check: Output = 8 x 24 = 192 W. Input = 240 x 1 = 240 W. Efficiency = 192/240 = 80 per cent.
frames.teach: The 12 V rating of each lamp is not needed: the wattage already tells you the power each one uses. Efficiency is always output over input.
frames.ask: Why can a transformer not work on DC?

frames.check: Because it needs a CHANGING flux to induce anything in the secondary. A steady direct current makes a steady flux, and a steady flux induces nothing. That is Faraday again.
frames.teach: Every induction question on this paper comes back to the same sentence: change is the whole word.

blocks.label: Your turn
blocks.question:
Fill each blank. These are the three fill-in-the-gap questions from Test 2, and every one is conceptual rather than numerical.

(1) Ampere's law is most useful for conductors with high ______.

(2) A changing magnetic ______ induces an emf.

(3) According to the Biot-Savart law, the magnetic field around a current element decreases with the square of the ______.
blocks.answer:
(1) symmetry. The law is always true but only SOLVABLE when you can pick a loop on which B is constant and along the path.

(2) flux, not field. Flux is BA cos θ, so rotating a loop in a steady field still induces an emf.

(3) distance. Biot-Savart falls as 1/r2, like Coulomb. Do not confuse it with the whole straight wire, which falls as 1/r because it sums every element along an infinite line.

blocks.big: Turns per metre, and change is the word
blocks.sub: Solenoid uses n = N/L; a steady flux induces nothing.
